report:
**Conclusion: Yes—offering HIV self-testing (HIVST) as an additional option generally increases HIV testing uptake**, especially among key populations and people who may not use facility-based testing. The strongest evidence comes from randomized trials and systematic reviews.

A 2021 systematic review of randomized trials found HIVST increased testing uptake overall compared with standard services (RR 2.09; 95% CI 1.69–2.58; 13 RCTs; moderate-certainty evidence): https://www.thelancet.com/journals/eclinm/article/PIIS2589-5370(21)00271-6/fulltext

A review focused on men who have sex with men and transgender people found HIVST increased testing uptake (RR 1.45; 95% CI 1.20–1.75), increased testing frequency, and was safe, without clear evidence of increased social harm: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-020-01835-z

A broader PLOS One review likewise concluded that HIVST increases uptake of HIV testing, while noting that linkage to confirmatory testing and care remains important: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0245498

The effect appears strongest when self-tests are **free, directly provided, and actively distributed**, rather than merely made available passively. In a Kenyan trial among female sex workers, direct provision was more effective than passive facility-based collection: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/A-Randomized-Controlled-Trial-to-Increase-HIV-Among-Kelvin-George/fba4e77ddfb5c6b496dbc98200cb897624bd38e5

Overall, adding HIV self-testing is an effective way to get more people tested, but programs should also support confirmatory testing and linkage to prevention or treatment.
